title: Mon, ma, mes: possessives
why: This lesson opens the unit on the people around you with the possessive adjectives and the vocabulary of the family. You'll learn the rule that trips up every English speaker: in French, the possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner.

My, your, our: the possessives

In English, “my” never changes: my brother, my sister, my parents. In French, the possessive is an adjective, so it agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows. You need three forms for most persons.

masculine nounfeminine nounplural noun
mymon frèrema sœurmes parents
your (tu)ton frèreta sœurtes parents
his / her / itsson frèresa sœurses parents
ournotre frèrenotre sœurnos parents
your (vous)votre frèrevotre sœurvos parents
theirleur frèreleur sœurleurs parents

For notre, votre and leur, masculine and feminine are the same: only the plural changes. In the plural, the final s is silent… except before a vowel, where you hear a liaison with a z sound: mes‿enfants, nos‿amis, leurs‿enfants.

Ton or votre?

The possessive follows your choice of tu or vous. With a friend: Comment s'appelle ta sœur ? With a stranger, someone older, or several people: Comment s'appelle votre sœur ? Mixing them (vous with ton) is a classic beginner's slip.

— Tu habites avec tes parents ? — Non, j'habite avec mon frère.— Do you live with your parents? — No, I live with my brother.
Madame, votre fils est dans la classe de Lucas ?Ma'am, is your son in Lucas's class?

Remember there is no “'s” in French: la sœur de Thomas = Thomas's sister. Once you know who you're talking about, the possessive takes over: sa sœur.

", "

The big trap: son, sa, ses

In English, “his” and “her” depend on the owner: a man's car is “his car”, a woman's car is “her car”. In French, son / sa / ses depend only on the thing owned. The owner doesn't matter at all.

Frenchcan meanbecause…
sa voiturehis car OR her carvoiture is feminine
son frèrehis brother OR her brotherfrère is masculine
ses enfantshis children OR her childrenenfants is plural
Thomas habite avec sa sœur.Thomas lives with his sister.
Léa adore son frère.Léa adores her brother.

Your English instinct will push you to say Léa et sa frère because Léa is a woman. Resist it: look at the noun, not the person. Context almost always tells you who the owner is. If you really need to insist, add a stressed pronoun: C'est sa voiture à elle (It's HER car).

Mon amie, not ma amie

Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel or a silent h, ma / ta / sa become mon / ton / son, simply to avoid two vowels clashing: mon amie, ton école, son adresse, mon histoire. The noun stays feminine: mon amie est canadienne. So mon ami and mon amie sound exactly the same: only the spelling shows the difference.

Leur or leurs?

Leur = their, with one thing; leurs = their, with several things: leur fille (their daughter, they have one), leurs enfants (their children). Don't use ses for several owners: Les enfants et leurs grands-parents, never ses grands-parents here.

", "

The family

Family words are learned in pairs. Note that several of them have two meanings, depending on the context.

MasculineFeminineEnglish
le pèrela mèrefather / mother
le frèrela sœurbrother / sister
le filsla filleson / daughter
le marila femmehusband / wife
le grand-pèrela grand-mèregrandfather / grandmother
l'onclela tanteuncle / aunt
le cousinla cousinecousin
le neveula niècenephew / niece
le conjointla conjointespouse, partner (official)
  • la femme = woman AND wife: une femme (a woman), ma femme (my wife).
  • la fille = girl AND daughter: une fille (a girl), sa fille (his or her daughter).
  • les parents = parents, but also relatives in general: J'ai des parents à Lyon can mean “I have relatives in Lyon”.
  • les beaux-parents = the in-laws (and also a stepfather and stepmother); les grands-parents = grandparents.
  • le fils is pronounced “feess”: the l is silent and the s is heard.

Talking about your family

— Tu as des frères et sœurs ? — Oui, j'ai un frère et deux sœurs.— Do you have any brothers and sisters? — Yes, I have one brother and two sisters.
Je suis fille unique. Mes parents habitent à Nice.I'm an only child (girl). My parents live in Nice.
Quel âge a ton fils ? Il a sept ans.How old is your son? He's seven.

“Brothers and sisters” is frères et sœurs, with no article in the question Tu as des frères et sœurs ?. English “siblings” has no everyday French equivalent.
